title: Who feeds me and heals me
hookLine: Ibrahim describes his Lord: who created me, guides me, feeds me, and heals me when I'm ill (26:78–80)
carry: he feeds me; he heals me

lines: BLOCK C: THE MIDDLE OF THE BOOK.
A SURAH OF PROPHETS AND A REFRAIN.
cards: Back to the book, and to its middle. This block opens with Surah Ash-Shu'ara, the Poets, the twenty-sixth. Ash-Shu'ara is long and full of prophets: Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb.
After each story comes the same refrain: in this is a sign, and your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Today's verses come from Ibrahim's story. He asks his father and his people what they worship.
Idols, they say, and their fathers did the same. And Ibrahim answers by describing, simply, the One he worships.

teach.b: Ibrahim's answer is made of verbs, and in Arabic nearly every one ends in the sound for me: created me, guides me, feeds me, heals me.
Pickthall: "Who created me, and He doth guide me, And Who feedeth me and watereth me. And when I sicken, then He healeth me."
He goes on: who causes me to die and then gives me life, and who, he hopes, will forgive his faults on the Day of Judgment.
Look at what he picks: not the stars or the mountains, but the things a person lives through every day. Being made. Being shown the way.
Breakfast. A glass of water. A fever that breaks.

teach.h: A THEOLOGY OF THE KITCHEN TABLE.
teach.b: It's a whole theology at the level of the kitchen table. Then a small detail in the grammar. Every line says He did it: He created, He guides, He feeds, He gives drink.
Until the illness. There Ibrahim doesn't say, when He makes me sick.
He says, when I sicken. Many commentators read that as adab, courtesy: he speaks of God in connection with the good, and takes the hard thing onto himself.
Not as a theory of where illness comes from, but as a way of speaking. The healing goes straight back to God.
The same shape runs through how many Muslims pray for the sick: the illness named plainly, the healing asked of God.
A hadith in Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, visiting the sick, asking God, the Healer, to heal, with a healing that leaves no illness behind.
The words are short, but they cover a life: made, guided, fed, given drink, healed, and in the end, he hopes, forgiven.

how: Many Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, and pray for the sick with words from the Prophet's practice that name God as the Healer.

o: a fever or illness sent as a test
a meal given to guests as charity
healing, which Ibrahim asks of his Lord

p: Ibrahim takes the hard thing on himself
the healing goes back to God

s: Ibrahim describes God mostly by the stars and mountains
he names daily things: being made, guided, fed, given drink, healed.
in the verse, Ibrahim says 'when I sicken', not 'when He makes me sick'
commentators read it as courtesy toward God.
it tells Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb, with a refrain after each.

games.q: you're Ibrahim. your people say they worship idols because their fathers did. how do you answer?
o: describe the One who made you, feeds you and heals you.
games.why: he describes his Lord through a life: created, guided, fed, given drink, healed, given death and life, and forgiveness he hopes for.

practice: Think about the last thing you ate and where it came from: the field, the hands that picked it, the truck, whoever cooked it.
Then go through Ibrahim's list slowly, made, guided, fed, given drink, healed, and stay with whichever one lands. If you pray, you can say thank you for it now.

wordCard.voice: Shifa'. Healing: what Ibrahim asks of his Lord in Ash-Shu'ara, the One who also made him, guides him, feeds him, and gives him drink. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'then He heals me', from shafa, to heal; the same root gives shifa', healing.

carryVoice: Your line: he feeds me; he heals me. The kitchen table, and the fever that breaks. That's day five hundred sixteen.
